title: Netanyahu Sidelined as Former Army Chief Gadi Eisenkot Tapped to Form Israeli Government
snippet: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has officially tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with building a new governing coalition, dealing a major blow to Benjamin Netanyahu following a chaotic parliamentary election.
content:
TEL AVIV — Israeli President Isaac Herzog has officially handed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form the country’s next government, delivering a sharp political blow to long-serving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after last month’s election left parliament deeply divided.

The announcement late Saturday capped days of intense consultations following the Oct. 27 vote, which saw Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc lose its governing majority in the 120-seat Knesset. While Herzog’s decision gives Eisenkot the strategic upper hand, it guarantees no easy path to assembling the 61-seat coalition required to take power.

A Fractured Parliament

Neither major political camp emerged from the voting booth with a clear mandate. Netanyahu’s coalition suffered a sharp collapse, dropping from 68 seats down to 53. Eisenkot’s opposition alliance captured 48 seats, while Arab-led political parties secured a historic 19 seats amid high turnout among Arab voters.

Herzog ultimately tapped Eisenkot after Arab-led parties indicated a willingness to support his bid to end Netanyahu’s tenure. However, translating that support into a viable governing coalition will require navigating intense ideological fault lines.

Eisenkot effectively faces three difficult options: striking a power-sharing deal with Netanyahu, persuading ultra-Orthodox parties to compromise on military draft exemptions, or relying on backing from Arab-led parties. The latter strategy faces strong resistance from conservative figures within Eisenkot’s own bloc, including the Yisrael Beytenu party.

At the same time, Eisenkot campaigned heavily on reforming Israel's conscription laws to end long-standing draft exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox community—a non-negotiable issue for religious factions like United Torah Judaism, whose support he may desperately need.

Netanyahu Pushes Back

Netanyahu has launched an aggressive pushback against the president's decision. The embattled leader has promoted unsubstantiated claims that the election was skewed by Arab voter turnout, warning that any Eisenkot-led alliance that depends on Arab political parties would represent a betrayal of the state.

While Israel's Shin Bet security agency is looking into potential foreign interference, election authorities and President Herzog have repeatedly affirmed the vote's validity, emphasizing that any minor irregularities had no bearing on the final outcome.

Netanyahu publicly called for a national unity government late Saturday, but commentators remain skeptical that the two fierce rivals can agree on a stable power-sharing framework.

The Road Ahead

Eisenkot will officially accept the presidential mandate on Sunday, kicking off a tight 28-day deadline to negotiate a deal, with the possibility of a two-week extension. If Eisenkot fails to lock down a 61-seat majority within six weeks, the mandate could revert to Netanyahu. Should both leaders fail to form a government, Israelis will likely head back to the polls for fresh elections next spring.

The newly elected Knesset will be sworn in Tuesday evening, while Netanyahu remains in power in a caretaker capacity with limited executive authority until a new coalition is finalized.
